strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and critical bottleneck in real-world V2X cooperative perception, namely the prohibitive communication, computational, and memory costs associated with full-precision models.

It provides a holistic, end-to-end quantized system design (QuantV2X) that targets both model-level quantization (PTQ for weights/activations) and communication-level quantization (via a learnable codebook indexing strategy).

The inclusion of a custom alignment module to mitigate feature distribution shifts (using KL-divergence) and spatial misalignment (using L2 loss over bounding boxes) represents a well-designed solution specifically tailored for multi-agent, multi-modal perception systems.

The experimental evaluation is highly detailed, leveraging both simulation (OPV2V) and real-world datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real). The hardware deployment profiling on TensorRT with custom CUDA plugins provides realistic latency and power consumption measurements, showcasing a high level of engineering maturity.
weaknesses: The system relies on a hybrid pipeline: while the network weights use Post-Training Quantization (PTQ), the communication component (Section 2.3) requires active model-wide joint optimization of the encoder, fusion, and head modules. This deviates from a purely calibration-only PTQ paradigm, and the paper should more explicitly highlight this training requirement.

The generalizability of the PTQ approach is constrained when applied to Transformer-based architectures. As shown in Table 1, V2X-ViT suffers a massive performance drop (from 57.4% AP30 down to 40.0% AP30 at 8/8 bits and 29.9% at 4/8 bits). Since Transformers are highly popular in current cooperative perception research, this limitation is significant.

In Table 3, the full-precision baselines are compared against compressed versions (e.g., 'x16 Compression'). The specific algorithm or autoencoder structure used to achieve this x16 baseline compression is not clearly detailed in the text, making it harder to evaluate the fairness of the communication baseline.

strengths: High Practical and System-Level Relevance: The paper tackles critical, real-world deployment challenges of V2X cooperative perception (such as high computation, memory, and communication bandwidth constraints) by proposing a fully quantized end-to-end system.

Comprehensive Full-Stack Solution: Instead of only optimizing model weights or the communication channel in isolation, QuantV2X holistically addresses both model-side computation (via post-training quantization) and communication-side feature transmission (via codebook-based message quantization).

Effective Calibration Alignment Module: To counter feature degradation and spatial misalignment caused by low-bit quantization in heterogeneous multi-agent settings, the authors introduce a calibration stage with heterogeneity alignment (KL-divergence) and spatial alignment (bounding box L2) losses, demonstrating solid accuracy recovery.

Thorough and Realistic Evaluation: The framework is validated across multiple datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V) and benchmarked using a real deployment-oriented platform (ROS and TensorRT), demonstrating a 3.2x end-to-end system latency reduction.
weaknesses: Incremental Technical Novelty on Components: Several core building blocks, such as the codebook-based feature compression (resembling CodeFilling) and the underlying PTQ techniques (like AdaRound), are adapted from existing literature. The main novelty lies in the holistic integration and the specific calibration alignment losses.

Severe Degradation on Transformer-based Architectures: As shown in Table 1, the performance of V2X-ViT drops drastically under low-bit quantization (e.g., AP30/50 from 57.4/49.5 to 29.9/8.8 for 4/8 bits). While the authors acknowledge this in the limitations, it indicates that the proposed PTQ method struggles with modern attention-based V2X fusion models.

Incomplete Individual Ablation of Alignment Losses: In Table 2, the ablation is shown sequentially (Max-min -> +AdaRound -> +L_hetero -> +L_spatial). A clean, non-cumulative ablation showing the isolated and joint impacts of L_hetero and L_spatial on top of the base quantization would provide clearer insights into their individual effectiveness.

strengths: Practical, systems-oriented motivation: The work addresses crucial bottlenecks in real-world V2X cooperative perception deployment, such as local computation latency, multi-agent communication bandwidth, and in-vehicle GPU memory constraints.

Comprehensive end-to-end recipe: Rather than only quantizing network weights, the paper presents a full-stack approach combining model quantization (PTQ) and transmission volume reduction (via a codebook representation), alongside feature/spatial alignment modules.

Extensive evaluations: The proposed method is evaluated across three major V2X datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V) and multiple fusion strategies (Pyramid Fusion, F-Cooper, AttFuse, etc.), showing robust accuracy preservation for CNN-based fusion methods.
weaknesses: Conceptual inconsistency regarding PTQ: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) is conventionally defined as quantizing a model without any retraining or weight adjustment. However, Section 2.3.2 describes a training stage where the encoder, fusion, and head are unfrozen and jointly optimized (Eq. 4). Presenting the system as a 'post-training quantization' process when it requires joint retraining/fine-tuning of the model is misleading.

Limited algorithmic novelty: The codebook-based transmission compression is highly similar to existing approaches like CodeFilling (Hu et al., 2024). The quantization techniques largely rely on off-the-shelf primitives (Max-min calibration, AdaRound). The proposed alignment losses ($L_{hetero}$ and $L_{spatial}$) during calibration are straightforward adaptations of standard teacher-student distillation (KL-divergence and L2-loss), leading to a somewhat incremental theoretical contribution.

Architecture-specific vulnerability: The method suffers from severe performance degradation on Transformer-based architectures. As shown in Table 1, on V2X-ViT, the AP30 drops drastically from 57.4% (FP32) to 29.9% (INT4/INT8). Since Transformer-based backbones represent the state-of-the-art in cooperative perception, this limitation seriously restricts the generalizability of the proposed framework.

Simulated communication latency: The paper reports a '3.2x system-level latency reduction'. However, the communication latency component ($T_{comm}$) is computed via a theoretical formula (using simulated transmission rates and arbitrary asynchronous delays) rather than measured over actual physical V2X network links. The framing of these simulated system-level improvements should be more carefully qualified.

Missing implementation details for reproducibility: Section D.1 mentions that custom CUDA kernels and TensorRT plug-ins were written to support quantization for specific network modules. However, the paper lacks technical descriptions, source code, or design details of these kernels, making it highly difficult to verify or reproduce the claimed local speedups.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and critical bottleneck in multi-agent V2X cooperative perception: the high computation, memory, and communication overhead associated with full-precision (FP32) intermediate feature maps.

Proposes a holistic end-to-end quantization pipeline (QuantV2X) that quantizes both the local/fusion model weights/activations (INT8/INT4) and the transmitted message representations (using learned codebooks to transmit low-bit code indices).

Introduces an alignment module with heterogeneity alignment and spatial alignment losses to explicitly resolve distribution shifts and spatial coordinate inaccuracies introduced by the quantization process.

Comprehensive evaluation on multiple V2X benchmarks (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V), real-world streaming frameworks (V2X-ReaLO), and hardware platforms (ROS, TensorRT plug-ins, RTX 3090 profiling for throughput and power).
Demonstrates excellent scalability under tight GPU memory budgets, enabling larger backbones to be deployed where full-precision baselines would otherwise exceed device limits.
weaknesses: The novelty of the communication compression scheme is somewhat incremental, as it heavily relies on the codebook-based messaging concepts established in prior works like CodeFilling [13]. The exact technical adjustments made specifically for the fully quantized setup could be more clearly highlighted.

The optimization process in Algorithm 1 is not fully explained. Specifically, lines 11 and 16 mention optimizing parameters $s_w, z_w, s_a,$ and $z_a$. It is unclear if backpropagation is used to update these calibration parameters, whether the model weights themselves are frozen, and what the exact training time overhead is for this block-wise calibration.

Although the post-training quantization (PTQ) method works well for CNN-based fusion approaches like Pyramid Fusion, Table 1 shows that attention-based methods (e.g., V2X-ViT) suffer from severe performance degradation under low-bit configurations (e.g., AP30 dropping from 57.4 to 29.9/8.8). This indicates the current quantization recipe still has limitations when generalizing to complex transformer architectures.

strengths: Practical and deployment-focused: The paper addresses the critical real-world bottlenecks of cooperative perception (on-board computation, memory, and transmission bandwidth) by proposing an end-to-end quantized system.

Convincing evaluation protocol: The paper evaluates the system using system-level latency-inclusive metrics, illustrating how the latency reduction of QuantV2X translates to massive improvements in practical performance (e.g., +9.5 mAP30) in dynamic environments over full-precision baselines.

Broad generalizability: The proposed PTQ method is shown to be effective across various fusion frameworks (Pyramid Fusion, F-Cooper, AttFuse, etc.) and heterogeneous sensor modalities (LiDAR, Camera).

Thorough physical validation: The authors deploy and validate their system on real-world platforms, utilizing the ROS-based V2X-ReaLO benchmark to measure actual end-to-end latency and power consumption.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The key technical building blocks are largely adapted from prior literature. The codebook-based feature compression is based on Hu et al. [13], the base PTQ leverages AdaRound [28], and the alignment module employs standard KL-divergence on features and L2 loss on box outputs to calibrate the network.

Unclear calibration optimization details: In Algorithm 1, lines 11 and 16 specify optimizing the quantization parameters ($s_w, z_w, s_a, z_a$) to minimize the alignment losses. It is unclear if the underlying model weights are frozen or if any auxiliary weight-rounding variables are updated. Additionally, optimizing quantization scales using a non-differentiable downstream detection head or complex loss might be highly non-convex; further explanation on the optimization stability and configuration would be helpful.

Key quantitative results pushed to the appendix: Highly informative tables that demonstrate the performance of individual components (like Table 10, showing alignment module results decomposed by distance and IoU thresholds) are placed in the appendix. Incorporating a condensed version of these tables into the main text would make the analysis more self-contained.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical and highly practical bottleneck in cooperative perception: the high latency, bandwidth, and memory constraints of deploying full-precision models on edge platforms.

It provides a comprehensive system-level evaluation, analyzing end-to-end latency, communication volume, memory footprint, and power consumption on physical hardware setups, rather than focusing solely on isolated offline accuracy.
The integration of model quantization (weight/activation) with communication quantization (transmitting codebook indices) represents a holistic full-stack approach to the V2X deployment challenge.
weaknesses: The paper blurs the line between Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) and Quantization-Aware Training (QAT). Although it claims to leverage a PTQ process to avoid retraining, Section 2.3 states that Stage 2 (Codebook Learning) unfreezes all parameters and performs joint optimization of the encoder, fusion module, and detection head. This makes the overall pipeline a hybrid QAT-PTQ framework, which compromises the standard data-efficiency and speed advantages of pure PTQ.

The algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental. Using shared codebooks and code indices to compress intermediate features in V2X has already been established by works like CodeFilling [13], and block-wise distillation for PTQ is widely adopted in existing literature (e.g., LiDAR-PTQ [55], Brecq [18]).

Several technical and mathematical details are unclear or lack formal definition. Specifically, Equation 9 defines the heterogeneity alignment loss using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence over continuous BEV feature maps ($H_i^{fp}$ and $H_i^{int}$). Since KL divergence is defined over probability distributions, the paper fails to explain how these continuous features are normalized or mapped into valid probability spaces. Similarly, Equation 10 does not define what constitutes 'bounding box representations' (e.g., regression targets, classification logits, or heatmaps) for the L2 loss calculation.

The performance gains over existing compressed communication baselines are marginal. In Table 3, when comparing the proposed QuantV2X to CodeFilling [13], the improvement in system-level accuracy is quite small (+1.2 mAP30 and +1.4 mAP50), raising questions about whether the added engineering complexity of full-network quantization and block-wise optimization is justified in practice.
